source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Epistemic Logic entry) on Hintikka (1962) Knowledge and Belief
finding: Hintikka gave the founding possible-worlds reading of knowledge. An agent knows p if p holds in every world the agent cannot tell apart from the actual one. His Partition Principle: any attitude splits worlds into those that fit it and those that do not. Built on von Wright (1951).
numbers: Semantics: w satisfies K_a p iff p holds at all w' with w R_a w'. No experiment; a formal theory.
limits: Entry is a secondary summary. Hintikka himself did not claim the model fits real people (see logical omniscience).
agent_relevance: Gives a precise definition of 'knows' as truth across a set of live possibilities. Background for any scaffold step that tracks what is still open.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Epistemic Logic entry) on Kripke models
finding: A Kripke model is worlds W, a relation R, and a valuation V. A pointed model adds the actual world. For knowledge R is an equivalence relation. Kripke (1963) semantics is the base for all later epistemic logics.
numbers: Model M=(W,R,V), W non-empty. Frame conditions: T=reflexive, B=symmetric, 4=transitive, 5=Euclidean, D=serial.
limits: Equivalence-relation (S5) reading is idealised; belief usually uses KD45.
agent_relevance: A runnable data structure: a set of candidate worlds with per-agent indistinguishability. Could be coded as a small checker.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Epistemic Logic entry) on axioms S5, KD45 and disputes
finding: S5 is the smallest normal logic with T, B and 4, and is the logic of equivalence-relation frames. KD45 is the usual belief logic (Fagin et al. 1995). Axiom 4 (KK) and 5 (negative introspection) are contested.
numbers: Hintikka accepted 4 on an autoepistemic argument but argued against 5. Williamson (2000, ch.5) rejects 4 by a margin-of-error argument. Choices of logic: von Kutschera 1976 S4.4, Lenzen 1978 S4.2, van der Hoek 1993 S4.3.
limits: No consensus logic of knowledge. Kraus and Lehmann (1986): combining KB1, KB3, D and 5 collapses knowledge into belief; van der Hoek (1993): none of the four can be dropped to stop the collapse.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'I know that I know' and 'I know what I do not know' are not safe defaults for self-checking steps. Metacognitive claims by the agent should not be assumed introspectively reliable.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Epistemic Logic entry) on logical omniscience
finding: In the standard model an agent knows every logical consequence of what it knows, including all theorems. Hintikka (1962, pp.30-31) already said this is inadmissible for real agents. Fixes: impossible worlds (Hintikka 1978), seemingly possible worlds (Rantala 1975).
numbers: Critics listed: Chisholm 1963, Hocutt 1972, Jago 2007.
limits: Fixes cost the clean semantics; no agreed bounded-reasoner logic.
agent_relevance: Direct match to LLM behaviour: a model neither knows all consequences nor none. The bounded reasoner is the right target, and budgeted derivation is what a scaffold supplies.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Epistemic Logic entry) on group knowledge operators
finding: Everybody knows E_G p = conjunction of K_i p. Distributed knowledge uses the intersection of relations. Common knowledge uses the reflexive transitive closure of the union of relations. No finite formula captures common knowledge, so it is a primitive operator.
numbers: R^D_G = intersection of R_i; R^C_G = (union of R_i)*. Early treatments: Lewis 1969, Aumann 1976, Lehmann 1984, Halpern and Moses 1984.
limits: Closure is an infinite conjunction of 'everyone knows that everyone knows...'.
agent_relevance: Tells us what a multi-agent or multi-instance setup would need: shared public facts versus facts each instance holds privately.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Modal Logic entry) on origins and Kripke semantics
finding: C. I. Lewis founded modal logic with strict implication to avoid paradoxes of material implication. Kripke (1963) semantics: box A is true at w iff A is true at every world R-accessible from w. K is the weakest normal system.
numbers: Frame <W,R>, W non-empty. Frame conditions: T reflexive; K4 transitive; KD serial; KD4 serial and transitive; S5 = S4 plus (5) or (B). Systems with completeness results listed: K, K4, KD, KD4, KC4, KDC4, S5, GL.
limits: The entry gives no complexity results. Lewis date 1918 and Kripke date 1959 are not in the text read.
agent_relevance: Modal operators are 'in all live cases'. This matches a scaffold step that checks a claim across all candidate readings.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Modal Logic entry) on correspondence and incompleteness
finding: Scott-Lemmon gave a wholesale correspondence between axioms of form (G) and frame conditions. Sahlqvist (1975) widened it. Correspondence is not always complete: H and GL express equivalent second-order conditions, yet H is incomplete.
numbers: Axiom schema (G) with hijk-convergence.
limits: Some modal logics are Kripke-incomplete.
agent_relevance: Background only; shows axioms can be read as constraints on the space of possibilities.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Dynamic Epistemic Logic entry) on public announcement logic
finding: PAL adds [F!]G, 'after announcing F, G'. An announcement deletes the worlds where F is false. Reduction axioms rewrite every announcement formula into a plain epistemic formula. After announcing p, p is common knowledge.
numbers: Reduction axioms: [F!]p <-> (F->p); [F!][a]G <-> (F->[a][F!]G). Reflexivity, transitivity, Euclideanness preserved; seriality not. Miller and Moss (2005): iterated announcement logic is not recursively axiomatizable.
limits: Plaza 1989 appears in the entry only for the sum-and-product puzzle; Gerbrandy 1999 only in passing.
agent_relevance: Learning from a truthful statement as world-elimination is a clean model for 'evidence prunes hypotheses'. It is a possible semantics for a verify step.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Dynamic Epistemic Logic entry) on action models and product update
finding: Baltag, Moss and Solecki (1998) action models: a finite set of events with agent relations and preconditions. Product update crosses the model with the action model. Handles private, semi-private and misleading announcements. Reduction theorem: every formula is equivalent to one without action models.
numbers: Worlds W[A]={(v,f): M,v satisfies pre(f)}; arrows kept iff both components related.
limits: Entry gives no empirical test of whether people follow these updates.
agent_relevance: Provides a formal way to represent who saw what; the core of theory-of-mind tasks where beliefs diverge from fact.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Dynamic Epistemic Logic entry) complexity table
finding: Reasoning cost rises fast with expressive power. Model checking of PAL and PAL with common knowledge is in P. Satisfiability of multi-agent PAL is PSPACE-complete; with common knowledge EXPTIME-complete; EAL satisfiability NEXPTIME-complete.
numbers: Single-agent PAL satisfiability NP-complete, Lutz 2006. EAL model checking PSPACE-complete, Aucher and Schwarzentruber 2013. PAL model checking in P, Kooi and van Benthem 2004.
limits: Worst-case results; typical puzzles are small.
agent_relevance: Model checking a given scenario is cheap while finding one is hard. This favours the pattern 'LLM proposes, small checker verifies'.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Dynamic Epistemic Logic entry) on belief change and Moore sentences
finding: Static belief change keeps the AGM Success postulate; dynamic belief change does not. The Moore formula (p and I do not know p) becomes false after it is announced, so Success fails. Plausibility models follow Baltag and Smets (2008).
numbers: Moore formula: p and not [a]p.
limits: Brief section in the entry.
agent_relevance: Warns that stating a fact about my own ignorance and then learning it changes the truth of the statement. Self-referring notes in a scratchpad can go stale.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Common Knowledge entry) on Lewis (1969) and Aumann (1976)
finding: Lewis (1969, Convention) gave the first full philosophical analysis of common knowledge. Aumann (1976) agreement theorem: agents with a common prior whose posteriors for an event are common knowledge must have equal posteriors.
numbers: Requires finite state space, positive prior probabilities, and the common prior assumption.
limits: Result fails without the common prior. The entry notes the term 'common knowledge' really concerns belief in Lewis's account.
agent_relevance: If agents share evidence and priors, persistent disagreement signals a missing shared step. Useful for multi-instance voting design.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Common Knowledge entry) on the muddy children (barbecue) puzzle
finding: With k messy diners, they act at the k-th ring of the bell. The announcement works by turning something all already know (when k>1) into common knowledge. Source of puzzle credited to Littlewood (1953).
numbers: k=1: acts at once. k=2: both act at ring 2. General: ring k.
limits: Experiments on humans are not in the text read.
agent_relevance: A standard test of iterated knowledge. Number of reasoning rounds equals nesting depth; a good diagnostic of depth limits.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Common Knowledge entry) on Rubinstein's e-mail game
finding: With any finite number of automatic confirmation messages, the only expected-utility-maximising choice is A for both players. They act as if no communication happened even with almost common knowledge.
numbers: States w1 prob 0.51, w2 prob 0.49; Lizzi observes the state, Joanna does not. Payoffs as printed by the entry: (A,A)=2, (B,B)=0, mismatch costs 0 or -4.
limits: Payoff figures are as the entry gave them and may differ from Rubinstein's original; check before reuse.
agent_relevance: Many rounds of 'I confirm' do not create shared certainty. A scaffold should not treat repeated self-confirmation as common knowledge.

source: Halpern and Moses (1990) Knowledge and Common Knowledge in a Distributed Environment
finding: Gave the formal framework for knowledge in distributed systems: individual, distributed and common knowledge. Showed common knowledge cannot be attained in practical systems with unreliable communication, and defined weaker attainable variants.
numbers: Journal of the ACM 37:3, pp. 549-587; first version 1984. Variants: eventual common knowledge, epsilon-common knowledge, timestamped common knowledge.
limits: Result holds for systems without guaranteed simultaneity.
agent_relevance: Turns knowledge talk into protocol design. Practical lesson: aim for attainable weaker states (eventual, timestamped) not perfect common knowledge.

source: Halpern and Moses (1990) on the muddy children puzzle
finding: If the father announces 'at least one is muddy' and k children are muddy, the first k-1 questions are answered no and the muddy children say yes at question k. If he does not announce, they never conclude. Announcing a fact all already know (k>1) adds E^(k-1) m to E^k m.
numbers: With k>1 every child initially knows m, but E^(k-1) m fails before the announcement; E^k m suffices for the muddy children to succeed.
limits: Assumes truthful, simultaneous, perfect reasoners.
agent_relevance: Shows the exact reasoning depth needed grows with k. An LLM that stops at depth 2 will fail for k>=3.

source: Halpern and Moses (1990) on the coordinated attack problem
finding: Two generals cannot guarantee a simultaneous attack over an unreliable messenger channel. Proof by induction on the number d of delivered messages: if k messages do not suffice, k+1 do not, because the sender of the last message cannot know it arrived. No k-round handshake works.
numbers: Problem from Gray (1978). Base case: zero messages delivered means B never learns of the plan.
limits: Assumes messages may be lost.
agent_relevance: Gives an impossibility result about agreeing on shared facts over lossy channels; relevant to any multi-agent handoff design.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Fitch's Paradox of Knowability) on Fitch 1963
finding: If every truth is knowable, every truth is known. Proof: instantiate knowability to p and not-Kp; K(p and not Kp) is impossible, so the assumption of an unknown truth fails. Referee of the 1945 version was identified in 2005 as Alonzo Church.
numbers: Premises KP, NonO; principles K(p and q) implies Kp and Kq, Kp implies p, necessitation. Fixes: Tennant 1997 (Cartesian), Dummett 2001 (basic statements), Edgington 1985 (actuality), intuitionistic (Williamson 1982), paraconsistent (Routley 1981; Beall 2000; Wansing 2002).
limits: The proof uses classical logic; most fixes restrict knowability or weaken the logic.
agent_relevance: Reminds us that 'unknown truths exist' and 'we can find out anything' cannot both be assumed. Do not promise exhaustive discovery.

source: Sileo and Lernould (2023) MindGames: Targeting Theory of Mind in LLMs with Dynamic Epistemic Modal Logic
finding: Built a controlled problem generator from DEL (SMCDEL model checker, S5): muddy-children style premises with public announcements and observability. Tested Pythia and GPT-3 families and GPT-3.5/GPT-4. Scaling did not beat chance zero-shot.
numbers: Dataset: 400 test cases per setup, balanced True/False, 4 setups. Pythia 70M-6.9B and GPT-3 350M-174B tested. Pythia scaling helps 5-shot but not 0-shot. Two NLP researchers: 94% accuracy, agreement 0.89. 20 sampled problems: GPT-3.5 60%, GPT-4 70%.
limits: Small qualitative GPT-4 sample (n=20). Models are old; no chain-of-thought tested. A shallow DeBERTa-small reached 83% on validation, which flags shortcuts.
agent_relevance: The first clean test that generated DEL problems expose weak epistemic reasoning. Generated, checkable problems are a way to test our own scaffold.

source: Sileo and Lernould (2023) MindGames problem design details
finding: Problems have up to 3 agents and hypotheses up to second-order. Negated knowledge predicates used 80% of the time in announcements to force richer inferences. Most human errors came from confusing 'know whether' with 'know that'.
numbers: N in {2,3,4} sampled, K=2, 11.2k train and 3.73k test/validation for the shortcut model.
limits: Evaluated by perplexity of True/False continuation, not free generation.
agent_relevance: Shows common surface confusions (whether vs that) that a scaffold prompt could name explicitly.

source: Sileo and Lernould (2023) vs Kosinski (2023) emergent theory of mind
finding: GPT-3 family showed no clear scaling trend on epistemic-logic items. The authors say the emergent theory-of-mind results reported by Kosinski (2023) were not due to robust epistemic logic capability.
numbers: Same standard prompting setup as Kosinski; lm-eval-harness.
limits: Argument is interpretive; they note failure on DEL examples does not prove absence of ToM.
agent_relevance: Sally-Anne style success may reflect surface cues, so passing ToM vignettes is weak evidence for tracking beliefs.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern and Zhang (2024) Conditional and Modal Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Tested 29 LLMs on valid and fallacious inference patterns with conditionals and epistemic might/must. All models make basic errors. Almost all accept the invalid patterns MuDistOr and MiAg. Many accept no-free-choice NSFC but reject WSFC while also accepting a standard equivalence, giving inconsistency.
numbers: 29 models; guessing accuracy 50%; accuracy on the uncontroversial patterns ranged roughly 45% to 89% across models (figure labels). Zero-shot, temperature 0, yes/no answers. Models do reason correctly about duality (not must = might not).
limits: Figure values read from labels in PDF text; exact per-model mapping not confirmed. Free-choice patterns are disputed in semantics.
agent_relevance: Shows 'might' and 'must' handling is fragile in the best models. Scaffold should check modal claims with explicit worlds.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern and Zhang (2024) correlations and prompting effects
finding: Model scores on these logic tasks correlate with Chatbot Arena Elo, MMLU and GSM8K. Zero-shot chain-of-thought reduced mistakes. Asking 'is this logically valid?' lowered acceptance of fallacies for some models.
numbers: 29 LLMs, error bars are 95% intervals. Compared zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought (Table 2).
limits: Few-shot examples used conjunction/disjunction items, not modals. A neurosymbolic parser does not handle these patterns automatically since theorem provers lack native support.
agent_relevance: Prompting for validity helps a bit; general capability predicts modal skill, so no cheap fix beyond tools.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) Belief in the Machine: KaBLE benchmark
finding: 13 tasks, 1,000 questions each, 13,000 total, 15 models, 195,000 queries. Models do well on true statements and badly on false first-person beliefs. Weak grasp that knowledge is factive.
numbers: Factual average 85.7% (92.1% confirming factual beliefs); false first-person belief confirmation 54.4% average; third-person false belief about 80.7%. GPT-4o 98.2% vs 64.4% (true vs false belief); GPT-4 93.4% vs 22.0%.
limits: Some false-scenario items in verification and recursive tasks have debatable answers under factivity. No human baseline reported.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that models fail to say 'you believe p' when p is false and they know it is false. Matters for any step that tracks the user's or its own beliefs.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) KaBLE gaps between true and false and between persons
finding: Large gaps by truth value. GPT-3.5: 89.8% vs 49.4% on direct fact verification and 93.2% vs 46.2% on personal belief. Claude 3 Haiku 93.4% vs 50.0%. Mixtral 8x22B 84.2% vs 18.8% on belief confirmation. Claude 3 Opus went the other way: 85.0% true vs 96.8% false on fact verification.
numbers: Distractor sentence raised accuracy 1.5 points on true and 11.7 points on false tasks. Zero-shot CoT on GPT-4o lowered direct fact verification by 6% and first-person belief by 4%.
limits: Gap not consistently related to size within families.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought is not a universal fix here; it can hurt simple verification tasks.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) KaBLE recursive knowledge tasks
finding: On 'James knows that Mary knows that p', confirmation is easy but verification and awareness drop. Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored 35.8% on verification and 0% on awareness, often answering undeterminable.
numbers: GPT-4o 95.0% verification, 83.4% awareness; Llama-3 70B 81.8% and 95.4%; confirmation 99.4% for GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Average across models: verification 78.4%, awareness 77.5%.
limits: Claude models demanded direct evidence of James's awareness; may reflect a pragmatic reading of 'knows'.
agent_relevance: Nested knowledge (the K-K axiom 4 in practice) is inferred unevenly; the agent should spell out the factivity step explicitly.

source: Suzgun et al. (2024) KaBLE factivity and 'really' effects
finding: Models wrongly challenge true knowledge claims, violating the truth axiom. Adding 'really' to first-person belief makes some models doubt (Llama-3 70B often answers no or undeterminable). Models seldom pick undeterminable for false knowledge claims.
numbers: GPT-4o rejected false first-person knowledge claims 72.4% of the time, 6.0% undeterminable; on direct fact verification of false claims 83.6% and 7.8%. Average response length: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 122 words vs 50 for GPT-4o.
limits: Footnote data from one model; wording-sensitive.
agent_relevance: Shows the model reasons from phrasing cues; scaffold should state the T axiom (knowledge entails truth) as a guardrail.
